It reaches 84.33% on FactKG using 108x fewer document tokens than full context. The post Stanford Research Open-Sources Memorilla, a Latent Memory Module for Frozen LLMs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Stanford researchers have released Memorilla , an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. On FactKG, a frozen Qwen3-8B scored 84.33% with Memorilla, against 80.43% with every document in context . It did that with 108x fewer document tokens. Code, training recipes and checkpoints are public under Apache 2.0 . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 194M-parameter trainable memory module. It always outputs 16 memory tokens, whatever the collection size. The encoder ( Qwen3-Embedding-4B ) and decoder ( Qwen3-8B ) stay frozen. Runs on: Linux with CUDA GPUs and Python 3.11. The quickstart needs 1 GPU with 80 GB (recipes ran on H100 80GB). No quantized variants disclosed. Performance: Highest reported average across 8 benchmarks (49.68), top score on 5 of 8. Best: PersonaMem-v2 accuracy of 44.60%, versus 27.92% for full context. Worst: PubMedQA accuracy of 59.00%, versus 69.00% for LLMLingua-2. What is Memorilla? Memorilla is a memory module that turns a document collection into 16 vectors for a frozen LLM. The work comes from Jure Leskovec’s SNAP group, with co-authors from Toronto, Penn and MIT. A frozen LLM can only use what sits in its context window. Full-context prompting grows slower as history grows. Retrieval pastes the chunks most similar to the question, and can miss weaker clues. Memorilla takes a third route: it learns what each question needs from the whole store. How does Memorilla work? The pipeline has 3 steps: Encode once. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B embeds each document a single time. New documents never force re-encoding of old ones. Read per question. 16 learned slots attend to the question and the full store. The module uses 2 cross-attention layers with 8 heads. Inject. The slots are projected into Qwen3-8B’s input embedding space and prepended to the question. Only the memory module trains: 194,123,776 parameters for the 8B decoder. Training runs in 3 stages. Stage 1 uses about 1.98M Wikipedia paraphrase-reconstruction examples. Stage 2 adds about 1.34M examples from 10 QA and summarization datasets. Stage 3 fine-tunes on all 8 benchmarks. The full recipe takes about 19 hours on 4 H100 GPUs. How does Memorilla perform on benchmarks? All baselines use the same frozen Qwen3-8B, per the paper’s main table. Scores are self-reported by the research team. FactKG: 84.33% accuracy, versus 80.43% full context and 80.38% MemoRAG. PersonaMem-v2: 44.60%, versus 30.90% for xRAG, the next best method. TriviaQA: 57.00 exact match, just ahead of MemoRAG at 56.60. LaMP-4 / LaMP-7: 18.15 and 48.37 ROUGE-L, both the best scores. Average: 49.68, versus 41.92 for xRAG, 40.75 for LLMLingua-2 and 38.02 for Mem0. Memorilla loses on 3 benchmarks. On PubMedQA it scores 59.00%, while LLMLingua-2 reaches 69.00%. Those abstracts total only 324 tokens, so compression has little to gain. MemoRAG leads on PersonalizationV4 (67.88% vs 66.65%) and NarrativeQA ROUGE-L (20.51 vs 19.31). MemoRAG used about 690x and 50x more document tokens there. Compression peaks on NarrativeQA: 16 tokens replace 67,385 document tokens, a 4,212x cut. As agent memory, 8 memory tokens lift a Qwen3-4B TextWorld agent from 18.6% to 24.2% average success. How fast is Memorilla compared to full context? On 1 H100, Memorilla answers in 0.74 s at 512 documents (about 128K tokens). Full context slows from 0.75 s to 19.9 s, which is 27x slower. The memory module itself takes about 2 ms. An optional memory cache precomputes cross-attention keys and values. On 1 B200, a question then takes 8.1 ms at 1M documents and 33 ms at 4M. With torch.compile , the 1M case drops to 5.0 ms. The cache costs 80 GiB at 4M documents. How do you run Memorilla? Install with uv on Linux, then load MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained . The first run downloads about 25 GB of models. Checkpoints live at memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B as Stage 1, 2, 3, PV4 and PMv2 folders. Each checkpoint must run with the decoder it was trained with ( evaluation docs ). Custom data needs parquet files with collection_id , question , answer and documents columns. The research team also released PersonalizationV4 : 149 synthetic users, 200 conversations each, under CC BY 4.0. Memorilla vs Mem0, MemoRAG and xRAG Benchmark scores come from Memorilla’s paper, which ran every baseline on the same Qwen3-8B. Licenses come from each project’s repository. FactKG: 84.33% vs 80.43% full context, with 108x fewer tokens. Highest reported 8-benchmark average: 49.68. Weak spot: PubMedQA at 59.00% and fine-grained facts.
